ta-l1prolq1-d1e96.summary: Aquinas's divisio and running gloss on Peter Lombard's prologue to the Sentences, followed by the announcement of the five questions on sacred doctrine. Using the rhetorical scheme of the exordium, he divides the prologue into three parts: Lombard renders the reader benevolent (by stating the causes moving him to compile the work), docile (by sketching the work's four causes), and attentive (by its usefulness, the depth of its matter, and its orderly method). The benevolence section is analyzed as a contest between three moving causes (desire to profit the Church, God's promise of reward and help, the requests of fellow students) and three restraining causes (his deficiency of knowledge and talent, the height of the matter and magnitude of the labor, the contradiction of the envious), in which zeal for the house of God wins; the first two moving causes show charity toward God, the third charity toward neighbor. Lemma by lemma, Aquinas glosses Lombard's images (the widow's mite, the gazophylacium as the study of Scripture, the Good Samaritan as God, the two denarii as the two Testaments, the tower of David as faith or the Church defended by the saints' arguments and authorities) and raises and resolves brief dubia: whether undertaking things beyond one's strength is forbidden (no, when one relies on divine help), whether 'praesumpsimus' implies sin, whether adding to Scripture is condemned (not when one unfolds what it implicitly contains), whether one can know one has charity (not as infused habit without revelation, but as intense love), whether truth can be hated (per accidens), and how false teachers can say true things (true in themselves but falsely used). He characterizes the adversaries as 'carnal' (those who deny providence and the soul's perpetuity in order to sin with impunity) and 'animal' (those who judge divine things by bodily reasons), and diagnoses opposition to truth as arising from a disordered will dragging reason after it. In the docility section he identifies the work's final cause (destruction of error and manifestation of truth), efficient cause (God principally, Lombard instrumentally as compiler), material cause (testimonies of truth), and formal cause (division into four books, method of examples and reasons). The paragraph ends by setting out the five questions that structure the ensuing quaestio: the necessity of sacred doctrine, its unity, whether it is practical or speculative (and if speculative, whether it is wisdom, science, or understanding), its subject, and its mode.
claims: Lombard's prologue follows the threefold structure of an exordium: making the reader benevolent, docile, and attentive.

Lombard's motives for compiling the Sentences manifest charity toward God (desire to profit the Church; trust in God's promised reward and help) and charity toward neighbor (yielding to the requests of fellow students).
Undertaking to contemplate what exceeds one's natural powers is not presumption when it relies on divine help rather than on one's own strength.
Adding to Scripture is blameworthy when one adds something contrary or alien, but laudable when one unfolds by exposition what Scripture contains implicitly.

No one can know with certainty without revelation that they possess charity as an infused habit, though they can conjecture it from probable signs; charity taken as intense love of the beloved can be known.
Truth is always loved in itself, but can be hated per accidens, and the accidental causes of such hatred are indefinitely many.
Resistance to truth arises from a disordered will that draws the judgment of reason after it, so that what pleases is judged true.
The Sentences have God as principal efficient cause and Lombard as instrumental cause, since the work is compiled from diverse authorities rather than invented.
The Sentences serve two purposes: the exclusion of error and the manifestation of truth, the latter concerning God and creatures in the first three books and the sacraments in the fourth.
Inquiry into sacred doctrine requires five questions: its necessity, its unity, its practical or speculative character, its subject, and its mode.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e838.summary: First objection of Article 1. Following Dionysius's definition of philosophy as knowledge of existing things, and noting by induction that philosophy treats every genus of being—creator and creatures, the works of nature and the works of human agency—the objection argues that since there can be no teaching except about existing things, no doctrine beyond the philosophical disciplines is needed.
claims: Philosophy, as knowledge of existing things, covers every genus of being, including the creator.
Since there is no science of non-being, no doctrine beyond philosophy has any remaining object.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e847.summary: Second objection of Article 1. Every doctrine aims at perfecting either the intellect (speculative sciences) or the affections as issuing in action (practical sciences); since philosophy already perfects the intellect through the demonstrative sciences and the affections through moral philosophy, no further doctrine is necessary.
claims: All doctrine perfects either intellect or affect.
Philosophy fully accomplishes both perfections, through demonstrative and moral sciences respectively.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e850.summary: Third objection of Article 1. Whatever can be known by natural reason is either contained in philosophy or discoverable from its principles, and natural knowledge suffices for human perfection. The minor premise is proved by a principle of nobility: what can reach its perfection by itself is nobler than what cannot; since other animals and even insensible creatures attain their ends by purely natural means (though not without God's general operation), man, being nobler, must be able to attain sufficient knowledge for his perfection through natural intellect.
claims: Whatever is naturally knowable is contained in or derivable from philosophy.
What attains its perfection by itself is nobler than what cannot.
Since lesser creatures reach their ends by natural means alone, the nobler human being should be able to do so by natural intellect.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e854.summary: First sed contra of Article 1. From Hebrews 11:6, that without faith it is impossible to please God, and the premise that pleasing God is supremely necessary, it argues that since philosophy cannot ascend to the things of faith, there must be a doctrine proceeding from the principles of faith.
claims: Pleasing God, which requires faith, is supremely necessary.
Philosophy cannot reach the objects of faith, so a doctrine proceeding from faith's principles is required.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e869.summary: Second sed contra of Article 1. An effect not proportioned to its cause leads only imperfectly to knowledge of that cause; every creature is such an effect with respect to the creator, from whom it is infinitely distant. Because philosophy proceeds only from reasons drawn from creatures, it is insufficient for knowledge of God, and a higher doctrine proceeding by revelation is needed to supply philosophy's defect.
claims: An effect disproportionate to its cause yields only imperfect knowledge of the cause.
Creatures are infinitely distant from and disproportionate to the creator.
Philosophy, proceeding from creaturely reasons, is insufficient for knowledge of God, so a revealed doctrine must supplement it.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e872.summary: The response of Article 1, which grounds the necessity of theology in the end of human life. All who have judged rightly hold that this end is the contemplation of God, which is twofold: an imperfect contemplation through creatures, in which the Philosopher placed contemplative happiness (a happiness of the wayfaring state) and to which all philosophy is ordered; and a perfect contemplation of God's essence immediately, attainable in patria and possible for man on the supposition of faith. Since means must be proportioned to the end, man must be led toward this second contemplation even in via by a knowledge not drawn from creatures but inspired immediately by divine light—this is theology. Two corollaries follow: theology commands all other sciences as principal, and it uses them in its service as vassals, as medicine commands and uses the work of the apothecary, because the end of all philosophy lies beneath and is ordered to the end of theology.
claims: The end of human life is the contemplation of God.
Contemplation of God through creatures is imperfect and constitutes only the happiness of the wayfarer, to which philosophy is ordered.
Immediate vision of God's essence is the perfect contemplation, possible for man on the supposition of faith.
Because means must be proportioned to their end, man requires in via a knowledge inspired by divine light rather than drawn from creatures, namely theology.
Theology commands all other sciences and uses them as subordinate servants, since the end of philosophy is ordered to the end of theology.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e875.summary: Reply to the first objection of Article 1. Granting that philosophy treats existing things, Aquinas distinguishes by the formality under which they are considered: philosophy considers them according to reasons drawn from creatures, while another doctrine must consider the same existents according to reasons received through the inspiration of divine light.
claims: The same existing things can be treated by different sciences according to different rationes.
Philosophy considers beings through creaturely reasons; theology considers them through reasons received by divine inspiration.
concepts: distinction of sciences by mode of consideration

ta-l1prolq1-d1e878.summary: Reply to the second objection of Article 1, drawn from the preceding solution. Philosophy perfects the intellect only according to natural knowledge and the affections only according to acquired virtue; another science is therefore required to perfect the intellect with infused knowledge and the affections with gratuitous love.
claims: Philosophy perfects intellect and affect only at the natural level.
A further science is needed for the supernatural perfection of intellect (infused knowledge) and affect (gratuitous charity).

ta-l1prolq1-d1e881.summary: Reply to the third objection of Article 1. The principle that what attains perfection by itself is nobler holds only among things that attain an equal good as their end. But, following the Philosopher, what attains a perfect good with many aids and motions is nobler than what attains an imperfect good with few or by itself. Man stands so with respect to other creatures, since he is made for participation in the divine glory itself; his need of help thus reflects the height of his end rather than inferiority.
claims: Self-sufficiency in attaining an end implies greater nobility only when the ends compared are equal.
Attaining a perfect good with many aids is nobler than attaining an imperfect good unaided.
Man's need for supernatural help reflects his higher end, participation in divine glory.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e893.summary: First objection of Article 2. Whatever man can be taught through creaturely reasons can also be taught through divine reasons; since the sciences proceeding by creaturely reasons are many and differ in genus and species (moral, natural, etc.), the sciences proceeding by divine reasons should likewise be many.
claims: The multiplicity of the philosophical sciences implies a corresponding multiplicity of sciences proceeding by divine reasons.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e896.summary: Second objection of Article 2. According to the Philosopher, one science is of one genus of subject; but God and creature, both treated in divine doctrine, cannot be reduced to one genus either univocally or analogically. The minor is proved: things sharing a genus univocally or analogically participate something common, whether by priority and posteriority (substance and accident in being) or equally (horse and ox in animal); but God and creature can participate nothing common, since that common item would be simpler than and prior to both.
claims: A single science requires a single genus of subject.
God and creature share no common genus, univocal or analogical, because anything common to both would be prior to and simpler than God.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e899.summary: Third objection of Article 2. Things produced by our agency (such as works of virtue) and things produced by nature belong to different sciences, moral and natural respectively. Since divine doctrine treats both—virtues and precepts on the one hand, angels and other creatures on the other—it seems not to be one science.
claims: Works of human agency and works of nature fall under distinct sciences.
Divine doctrine treats both kinds of object, and so seems not to be one science.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e903.summary: First sed contra of Article 2. Whatever agrees in one ratio can belong to one science, as all things belong to metaphysics insofar as they agree in the ratio of being. Divine science treats things according to the divine ratio, which embraces everything since all things are from God and toward God; therefore it can be one while being about diverse things.
claims: Unity of science follows unity of the ratio under which things are considered.
Divine science considers all things under the divine ratio, since all things are from and toward God, and so can remain one while treating diverse things.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e906.summary: Second sed contra of Article 2, from the literary form of Scripture. Matters belonging to different sciences are treated separately in different books, but sacred Scripture treats morals, the creator, and creatures intermixed within the same book; hence this variety of topics does not diversify the science.
claims: The intermixture of moral, theological, and cosmological topics within single books of Scripture indicates that they belong to one science.
concepts: literary form as evidence of unity

ta-l1prolq1-d1e909.summary: The response of Article 2. The higher a cognition is, the more unified it is and the more things it extends to; thus God's intellect, through the light that is God himself, knows all things distinctly. Likewise this science, being highest and drawing its efficacy from the light of divine inspiration, remains one and unmultiplied while considering diverse things—not merely in common, as metaphysics considers all things as beings without descending to proper knowledge of moral or natural things, but in their specific character. The ratio of being, being diversified in diverse things, is insufficient for special knowledge, whereas the divine light, remaining one in itself (as Dionysius says), is efficacious for manifesting them.
claims: The higher a cognition, the more unified it is and the wider its extension.
Sacred doctrine, as the highest science and grounded in divine inspiration, remains one while treating diverse things.
Unlike metaphysics, which knows all things only in common under the ratio of being, sacred doctrine can extend to proper knowledge of moral and natural things.
The divine light, one in itself, is efficacious for the distinct manifestation of many things.
concepts: theology as impressio of divine science

ta-l1prolq1-d1e912.summary: Reply to the first objection of Article 2. The divine light from whose certitude this science proceeds is efficacious for manifesting the many things that the various philosophical sciences treat by proceeding from their own reasons; therefore this science need not be multiplied to match them.
claims: The single divine light suffices to manifest what the many philosophical sciences treat separately, so sacred doctrine need not be multiplied.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e915.summary: Reply to the second objection of Article 2. Creator and creature are reduced to one not by univocal community but by analogy, which is of two kinds: one where several things participate something one by priority and posteriority (as potency and act, or substance and accident, in the ratio of being), and one where one thing receives its being and ratio from another. The analogy of creature to creator is of the second kind: the creature has being only as descending from the first being and is called a being only insofar as it imitates the first being; and likewise for wisdom and every other name said of creatures. This avoids positing any common item prior to God.
claims: Creator and creature are unified by analogy, not univocity.
Analogy may be by common participation in something one according to prior and posterior, or by one thing's receiving being and ratio from another.
The analogy of creature to creator is of the second kind: the creature is a being only by descending from and imitating the first being.
The same holds for wisdom and all other perfections predicated of creatures.
concepts: analogy of participation vs. analogy of attribution/imitation

ta-l1prolq1-d1e918.summary: Reply to the third objection of Article 2. Works of human agency and works of nature, considered according to their proper rationes, do not fall under the same doctrine; yet one science, having certitude through the divine light that is efficacious for knowing both, can consider both. Alternatively, the virtue the theologian considers is not from our agency at all, since, as Augustine says, God works it in us without us.
claims: Moral and natural objects considered under their proper rationes belong to different sciences, but both can be considered by one science under the divine light.
The virtue considered by theology is infused, worked by God in us without us, and so is not strictly a work of human agency.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e935.summary: Objection opening Article 3, quaestiuncula 1: sacred doctrine seems to be practical. The end of practical science is action, per the Philosopher; and this doctrine, which belongs to faith, is principally for acting well, as James 2:26 (faith without works is dead) and Psalm 110:10 (good understanding to all who do it) indicate.
claims: Practical science is defined by having action as its end.
The doctrine of faith seems principally ordered to good action, and so seems practical.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e966.summary: First sed contra of quaestiuncula 1: the Philosopher says the noblest of the sciences is for its own sake; practical sciences are not for their own sake but for action; since this is the noblest of sciences, it is not practical.
claims: The noblest science is pursued for its own sake.
Practical sciences are for the sake of action, so the noblest science is not practical.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e969.summary: Second sed contra of quaestiuncula 1: practical science treats only what comes from our agency, but this doctrine considers angels and other creatures not produced by us; therefore it is speculative rather than practical.
claims: Practical science is restricted to objects produced by human agency.
Since sacred doctrine treats angels and other creatures not made by us, it is speculative.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e978.summary: First objection of quaestiuncula 2, on whether sacred doctrine is a science: per the Philosopher there is no science of particulars, but sacred Scripture recounts the deeds of particular men such as Abraham and Isaac; therefore it is not a science.
claims: Science is not of particulars.
Scripture narrates particular deeds, and so seems not to be a science.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e984.summary: Second objection of quaestiuncula 2: every science proceeds from self-evident principles manifest to anyone, but this one proceeds from credibles that are not granted by all; therefore it is not a science.
claims: Science requires principles self-evident to all.
Sacred doctrine proceeds from articles of belief not universally granted, and so seems not to be a science.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e987.summary: Third objection of quaestiuncula 2: in every science some habit is acquired through the reasons adduced, but in this doctrine no habit is acquired, since faith, on which the whole doctrine rests, is not an acquired but an infused habit; therefore it is not a science.
claims: Every science produces an acquired habit through argument.
Faith, the foundation of sacred doctrine, is infused rather than acquired, so this doctrine seems to yield no acquired habit.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e990.summary: Sed contra of quaestiuncula 2: according to Augustine, theology is the science of the things pertaining to human salvation; therefore it is a science.
claims: On Augustine's authority, theology is a science of the things pertaining to salvation.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e999.summary: Objection of quaestiuncula 3, on whether sacred doctrine is wisdom: per the Philosopher, the wise man must be most certain of causes; but no one in this doctrine is most certain, since faith, on which it rests, is below science and above opinion; therefore it is not wisdom.
claims: Wisdom requires the highest certainty about causes.
Faith, standing between science and opinion, lacks the highest certainty, so sacred doctrine seems not to be wisdom.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1002.summary: Sed contra of quaestiuncula 3: from 1 Corinthians 2:6, 'we speak wisdom among the perfect'; since the Apostle taught and spoke of this doctrine, it seems to be wisdom.
claims: The Apostle's description of his teaching as wisdom indicates that sacred doctrine is wisdom.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1023.summary: The unified response to quaestiuncula 1, which also lays the ground for quaestiunculae 2 and 3. Though one, this science is perfect and sufficient for all human perfection through the efficacy of the divine light, perfecting man both in right action and in contemplation of truth, and so is in some respect both practical and speculative. But since every science is to be judged principally by its end, and the ultimate end of this doctrine is the contemplation of the first truth in patria, it is principally speculative. Among the three speculative habits (wisdom, science, understanding), it is wisdom, because it considers the highest causes and is head, principal, and orderer of all sciences—even more properly wisdom than metaphysics, since it considers the highest causes in the manner of those causes themselves, through inspiration received immediately from God, whereas metaphysics considers them through reasons taken from creatures. Hence it is more divine than metaphysics, being divine both in subject and in mode of reception. And because wisdom considers both conclusions and principles, it also includes science and understanding.
claims: Sacred doctrine, though one, perfects man both in action and in contemplation, and so is in a sense both practical and speculative.
A science is to be characterized principally by its end; since the ultimate end of sacred doctrine is contemplation of the first truth in patria, it is principally speculative.
Sacred doctrine is wisdom because it considers the highest causes and orders all sciences.

Sacred doctrine is more properly wisdom and more divine than metaphysics, since it knows the highest causes through divine inspiration rather than through creaturely reasons, being divine in mode as well as subject.
Because wisdom treats both principles and conclusions, sacred doctrine also comprises science and understanding.
concepts: specification of a science by its end

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1026.summary: Reply to the objection of quaestiuncula 1. Action is not the ultimate aim of this science; rather, its ultimate aim is the contemplation of the first truth in patria, which we reach after being purified by good works (Matthew 5:8, 'blessed are the pure of heart'). Good works are thus subordinated to contemplation, and the science is more principally speculative than practical.
claims: The ultimate end of sacred doctrine is contemplation of the first truth, not action.
Good works serve as purification toward that contemplation, so practice is subordinate to speculation in this science.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1043.summary: A brief formula concluding the response to quaestiuncula 1, conceding the two sed contra arguments (that the noblest science is for its own sake, and that sacred doctrine treats things not made by us) as supporting its principally speculative character.
claims: The two arguments for the speculative character of sacred doctrine are granted.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1052.summary: Determination of quaestiuncula 2: sacred doctrine is a science. The bare assertion relies on the preceding response, where it was shown to include science as a part of wisdom, and introduces the replies that follow.
claims: Sacred doctrine is a science.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1055.summary: Reply to the first objection of quaestiuncula 2. Sacred doctrine treats particulars not insofar as they are particulars but insofar as they are examples of what is to be done; moral science does the same, since actions concern particulars and moral matters are better manifested through particular examples.
claims: Scripture treats particular persons and deeds as exemplars for action, not as particulars as such.
Use of particular examples is also proper to moral science, since actions concern particulars.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1058.summary: Reply to the second objection of quaestiuncula 2, articulating theology's scientific structure. Sacred doctrine has as its first principles the articles of faith, which are self-evident to one who has faith through the infused light of faith, just as naturally implanted principles are known through the light of the agent intellect. It is no wonder that unbelievers do not know them, since even natural principles would be unknown without the light of the agent intellect. From these principles—without rejecting common principles—the science proceeds; it has no way to prove them but only to defend them against those who contradict them, as no practitioner of an art can prove the art's own principles.
claims: The articles of faith function as the first principles of sacred doctrine.
The articles are per se nota to the believer through the infused light of faith, analogously to how natural principles are known through the light of the agent intellect.
The unbeliever's ignorance of the articles no more undermines theology's scientific status than ignorance of natural principles would without the agent intellect.
Sacred doctrine also makes use of common principles of reason.
Sacred doctrine cannot prove its principles but can defend them against objections, as every science or art presupposes its own principles.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1061.summary: Reply to the third objection of quaestiuncula 2. Just as the habit of first principles is not acquired through other sciences but given by nature, while the habit of conclusions deduced from them is acquired, so in this doctrine the habit of faith, which functions as a habit of principles, is not acquired, but there is acquired the habit of what is deduced from the articles and of what serves their defense.
claims: Faith in sacred doctrine corresponds to the habit of first principles, which is not acquired by argument.
Theology acquires a habit concerning the conclusions deduced from the articles and the arguments defending them.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1065.summary: A brief formula concluding the response to quaestiuncula 2, conceding the sed contra argument from Augustine that theology is a science.
claims: The Augustinian argument that theology is a science is granted.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1074.summary: Determination of quaestiuncula 3: sacred doctrine is most properly wisdom, as already established in the response to quaestiuncula 1.
claims: Sacred doctrine is wisdom in the most proper sense.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1077.summary: Reply to the objection of quaestiuncula 3, on the certitude of faith. It is false that no one is most certain in this doctrine: the believer assents more firmly to the things of faith than even to the first principles of reason. The claim that faith is below science refers not to infused faith but to acquired faith, which is opinion strengthened by reasons. The habit of the articles is called faith rather than understanding because these principles are above reason, which cannot fully grasp them; the resulting knowledge is deficient not through lack of certainty in what is known but through a defect in the knower. Yet reason, led by faith, grows so as to comprehend the credibles more fully and in a way understand them—hence Isaiah 7:9 in the other version: 'unless you believe, you will not understand.'
claims: The believer's assent to the articles of faith is firmer than assent to the first principles of reason.
The dictum that faith is below science applies to acquired faith (opinion strengthened by reasons), not to infused faith.
The habit of the articles is called faith rather than understanding because its principles exceed reason.
The deficiency of faith-knowledge lies in the knower, not in the certainty of the objects known.
Reason guided by faith grows toward a fuller comprehension and a certain understanding of the credibles.
concepts: certitude of object vs. of subject

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1106.summary: First objection of Article 4, with its own counter-argument. Since every science is entitled and named from its subject, and this science is called theology ('speech about God'), God seems to be its subject. Against this, Boethius says a simple form cannot be a subject; God is such a form; so God cannot be the subject.
claims: A science is named after its subject, and 'theology' names God, so God seems to be its subject.
On Boethius's principle that a simple form cannot be a subject, God cannot be the subject of a science.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1109.summary: Second objection of Article 4, with counter-argument. Following Hugh of St Victor, who says that the works of the first foundation are the matter of other sciences and the works of restoration the matter of theology, the works of restoration seem to be the subject. Against this, whatever a science determines must fall under its subject, yet theology treats the works of creation (Genesis 1), so the works of restoration cannot be its subject.
claims: Hugh of St Victor assigns the works of restoration to theology as its matter.
Since theology also treats creation, which is not a work of restoration, restoration cannot be its comprehensive subject.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1123.summary: Third objection of Article 4, with counter-argument. The subject is that around which the whole intention of a science turns; the Master of the Sentences says theology's whole intention concerns things and signs; so things and signs are its subject. Against this, a science must be distinguished from others by its subject, but other sciences also treat things and signs, so they cannot be theology's proper subject.
claims: Following Lombard's Augustinian scheme, things and signs seem to be the subject of theology.
Because other sciences also treat things and signs, they cannot be the proper, distinguishing subject of theology.
concepts: subject as principle of distinction of sciences

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1127.summary: The response of Article 4. A subject has at least three relations to its science: (1) everything in the science must be contained under it—on this basis some posited things and signs, others the whole Christ, head and members, as theology's subject; (2) knowledge of the subject is principally intended—on this basis some posited God; (3) the subject distinguishes the science from all others—on this basis some posited the credible (since theology proceeds by inspiration of faith), others the works of restoration (since the whole science is ordered to the effect of restoration). Each prior position thus captures one condition. Seeking a subject that satisfies all three, Aquinas proposes 'divine being knowable through inspiration' (ens divinum cognoscibile per inspirationem): everything considered in this science is either God or what is from God and toward God as such, just as the physician considers signs and causes insofar as they relate to health. Accordingly, the closer something comes to the true ratio of divinity, the more principally it is considered in this science.
claims: A science's subject must contain everything treated in it, be what is principally known, and distinguish the science from others.
Previous proposals (things and signs, the whole Christ, God, the credible, the works of restoration) each satisfy only one of these conditions.
The subject of sacred doctrine, satisfying all three conditions, is divine being knowable through inspiration.
Everything treated in theology is either God or things from and toward God considered as such, as medicine treats everything under its relation to health.
Things are treated more principally in theology the closer they approach the true ratio of divinity.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1130.summary: Reply to the first objection of Article 4 and its counter-argument. God is the subject only as what is principally intended and as the ratio under which everything in the science is considered. As for Boethius's claim that a simple form cannot be a subject, this is true of being a subject of accidents; but a simple form can still be the subject of a predicate in a proposition, and whatever can be such can be the subject of a science provided that predicates can be proved of it.
claims: God is the subject of theology as principally intended and as the formal ratio under which all is considered.
Boethius's principle concerns being a subject of accidents, not being a logical subject of predication.
Whatever can be a subject of predication can be the subject of a science, provided predicates can be demonstrated of it.
concepts: subject of accidents vs. subject of predication

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1133.summary: Reply to the second objection of Article 4: the works of restoration are not properly the subject of this science, except insofar as everything said in it is in some way ordered to our restoration.
claims: The works of restoration are the subject of theology only in the qualified sense that everything in theology is ordered to our restoration.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1136.summary: Reply to the third objection of Article 4: things and signs taken generally are not the subject of this science, but only insofar as they are in some way divine.
claims: Things and signs belong to theology's subject only insofar as they are divine.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1148.summary: First objection of Article 5. The noblest science should have the noblest mode, and the more artful (artificialis) a mode, the nobler; since this science is the noblest, its mode should be most artful—implicitly, more rigorously systematic than Scripture's actual manner of proceeding.
claims: The noblest science should have the most artful mode of proceeding.
A more artful mode is a nobler mode.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1151.summary: Second objection of Article 5. A science's mode should be proportioned to it; since this science has been proved to be supremely one, its mode should be supremely one; yet it proceeds in many modes—sometimes threatening, sometimes commanding, and otherwise.
claims: The unity of a science requires a single mode of proceeding.
Sacred doctrine's multiple modes seem incompatible with its demonstrated unity.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1154.summary: Third objection of Article 5. Sciences that differ most should not share a mode; poetics, containing the least truth, differs most from this science, which is truest; since poetics proceeds by metaphorical locutions, this science should not.
claims: Maximally different sciences should not share a mode.
Since poetics uses metaphor and is least true, the truest science should not use metaphor.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1158.summary: Fourth objection of Article 5. Ambrose says 'take away arguments where faith is sought'; since faith is supremely sought in sacred science, its mode should in no way be argumentative.
claims: Because faith excludes argument, sacred science should not proceed argumentatively.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1167.summary: First sed contra of Article 5. 1 Peter 3:15 commands believers to be ready always to give an account of the hope that is in them; this cannot be done without arguments; therefore sacred doctrine must sometimes use arguments.
claims: Giving an account of one's hope requires arguments, so sacred doctrine must at times argue.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1178.summary: Second sed contra of Article 5, confirming the first: Titus 1:9 requires that the teacher be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it, which again implies the use of argument.
claims: The office of teaching includes refuting opponents, which requires argument.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1188.summary: The response of Article 5, a systematic derivation of the multiple modes of sacred doctrine from the conditions of its matter (per Boethius and Aristotle). Because its principles are received by revelation, the mode of receiving them is revelatory on the part of the one infusing (as in the prophets) and prayerful on the part of the recipient (as in the Psalms). Because the habit of faith must be determined to specific credibles by preaching, and the preacher's truth is confirmed by miracles, the mode must be narrative of signs. Because these principles exceed reason in via, which learns from sensibles, the mode must be metaphorical, symbolic, or parabolic. From these principles Scripture proceeds to three ends: the destruction of errors, requiring an argumentative mode (by authorities, reasons, and natural similitudes); the instruction of morals, requiring preceptive (law), threatening and promising (prophets), and narrative-of-examples (histories) modes; and the contemplation of truth in questions, again argumentative, as in the writings of the saints and in this book compiled from them. Correspondingly, there is a fourfold sense of Scripture: historical (the truth of faith itself), moral (instruction of morals), allegorical (contemplation of truths of the way), and anagogical (contemplation of truths of the homeland). Only the literal sense serves for refuting errors, since the other senses are taken through similitudes and no argument can be drawn from figurative speech—as Dionysius says, symbolic theology is not argumentative.
claims: The mode of a science must be determined by the conditions of its matter.
Since sacred doctrine's principles are revealed, its mode of receiving them is revelatory on God's side and prayerful on the human side.
Since faith is specified through preaching confirmed by miracles, sacred doctrine must narrate signs.
Since its principles exceed reason in via, which learns from sensibles, sacred doctrine must use metaphor and symbol.
Sacred doctrine proceeds from its principles to three ends—refuting error, instructing morals, and contemplating truth—each requiring its appropriate modes.
The fourfold sense of Scripture (historical, moral, allegorical, anagogical) corresponds to the ends to which the doctrine proceeds.
Only the literal sense can ground argument against error, since symbolic theology is not argumentative.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1219.summary: Reply to the first objection of Article 5. A mode is called artful insofar as it befits its matter, so that what is artful in geometry is not artful in ethics; accordingly, the mode of this science is supremely artful precisely because it is supremely suited to its matter. The reply redefines 'artful' relative to subject matter rather than formal rigor.
claims: A mode is artful insofar as it fits its matter, not by an absolute standard.
The mode of sacred doctrine is supremely artful because it is supremely fitted to its matter.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1222.summary: Reply to the second objection of Article 5: although this science is one, it concerns many things and avails for many ends, according to which its modes must be multiplied, as the response has shown.
claims: The unity of sacred doctrine is compatible with a plurality of modes, which follows from the plurality of its objects and ends.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1226.summary: Reply to the third objection of Article 5. Poetics concerns things that, through a deficiency of truth, cannot be grasped by reason, so reason must be led by certain similitudes; theology concerns things above reason. Hence the symbolic mode is common to both because neither is proportioned to reason—one falls below it, the other exceeds it.
claims: Poetic matter falls below reason through defect of truth; theological matter exceeds reason.
The symbolic mode is common to poetics and theology because neither matter is proportioned to reason, though for opposite reasons.

ta-l1prolq1-d1e1229.summary: Reply to the fourth objection of Article 5. Arguments are excluded for proving the articles of faith, but for defending the faith and for discovering truth in questions from the principles of faith, arguments must be used—as the Apostle does in 1 Corinthians 15, arguing from Christ's resurrection to the resurrection of the dead.
claims: Arguments cannot prove the articles of faith.
Arguments are legitimately used to defend the faith and to draw out truths from its principles, as Paul does regarding the resurrection.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e930.summary: The objections and counter-arguments of the first quaestiuncula of Article 3: whether sacred doctrine is practical or speculative. A single objection argues that it is practical, since faith is principally ordered to good works (James 2:26). Two sed contra arguments answer that it is speculative: the noblest science is pursued for its own sake, and practical science treats only what we produce, whereas this doctrine also treats angels and other creatures. The determination is deferred to the later Responsio section.
claims: Sacred doctrine's orientation to good works suggests it is practical.
Its nobility and its treatment of things not made by us suggest it is speculative.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e973.summary: The objections and counter-argument of the second quaestiuncula of Article 3: whether sacred doctrine is a science in the Aristotelian sense. Three objections deny it: science is not of particulars, yet Scripture narrates particular deeds; science proceeds from principles self-evident to all, yet this doctrine proceeds from credibles not granted by all; science produces an acquired habit, yet faith, its foundation, is infused. Against these, Augustine calls theology the science of things pertaining to salvation.
claims: Sacred doctrine's treatment of particulars, its non-evident principles, and its basis in infused faith seem to exclude it from being a science.
On Augustine's authority, theology is a science.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e994.summary: The objection and counter-argument of the third quaestiuncula of Article 3: whether sacred doctrine is wisdom. The objection holds that wisdom requires the highest certainty about causes, while faith, the basis of this doctrine, lies below science and above opinion. The sed contra cites 1 Corinthians 2:6, where the Apostle speaks of wisdom among the perfect.
claims: The lesser certainty of faith seems to keep sacred doctrine from being wisdom.
Paul's description of his teaching as wisdom indicates that it is wisdom.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e1018.summary: The response to the first quaestiuncula of Article 3. Sacred doctrine, one but perfect through the divine light, perfects human beings in both action and contemplation, and so is in a way both practical and speculative. But it is principally speculative, because a science is judged by its end and this doctrine's ultimate end is contemplation of the first truth in patria, to which good works are only a purification (Matthew 5:8). Among the speculative habits it is wisdom, more properly so and more divine than metaphysics, because it knows the highest causes through immediate divine inspiration rather than through creaturely reasons. Since wisdom treats principles and conclusions, it also includes science and understanding. The two sed contra arguments are conceded. This response also provides the basis for answering the two following quaestiunculae.
claims: Sacred doctrine is both practical and speculative, but principally speculative, because its ultimate end is contemplation of the first truth.
Sacred doctrine is wisdom, more properly and more divinely than metaphysics, since it knows the highest causes by divine inspiration.
As wisdom, it includes both science and understanding.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e1047.summary: The response to the second quaestiuncula of Article 3 which sets out Aquinas's account of theology as a science grounded in the principles of faith. Sacred doctrine is a science. It treats particulars as exemplars for action, as moral science does. Its first principles are the articles of faith, which are self-evident to the believer through the infused light of faith, as natural principles are known through the agent intellect; it cannot prove these principles but can defend them, as every art presupposes its own. And just as the habit of first principles is natural while the habit of conclusions is acquired, faith here is unacquired while theology acquires a habit of the conclusions drawn from the articles and of their defense. Augustine's sed contra is conceded.
claims: Sacred doctrine is a science.
Its use of particulars is exemplary, as in moral science.
The articles of faith are its first principles, self-evident to the believer by the light of faith.
It does not prove its principles but defends them, and it acquires a habit of conclusions deduced from them.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e1069.summary: The response to the third quaestiuncula of Article 3: sacred doctrine is most properly wisdom. Against the objection that it lacks the highest certainty, Aquinas argues that the believer assents more firmly to the articles than to the first principles of reason. The dictum that faith is below science concerns acquired faith, not infused faith. The habit of the articles is called faith rather than understanding because they exceed reason. Its deficiency lies in the knower, not in the certainty of what is known. Yet reason led by faith grows toward a certain understanding of what is believed (Isaiah 7:9).
claims: Sacred doctrine is most properly wisdom.
The certainty of infused faith exceeds even that of the first principles of reason.
Faith's deficiency is on the side of the knower, not the certainty of its object.
Reason guided by faith progresses toward understanding.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e830.summary: Article 1 asks whether, besides the philosophical disciplines, another doctrine is necessary for human beings. The objections argue that philosophy is sufficient: it covers every genus of being, perfects both intellect and affect, and man, nobler than other creatures, should reach his end by natural means. The sed contra arguments respond that faith is necessary to please God and that creatures, being disproportionate effects, lead only imperfectly to knowledge of God. In the response, Aquinas grounds the necessity of theology in the end of human life. That end is the contemplation of God, which is either imperfect, through creatures (the philosophers' felicity of the way), or perfect, by immediate vision of the divine essence in patria. Since means must be proportioned to their end, a knowledge inspired by divine light is needed in via, and this is theology. Theology therefore commands all other sciences and uses them as servants. The replies hold that philosophy and theology treat the same beings under different rationes, and that theology supplies infused knowledge and gratuitous love where philosophy gives only natural knowledge and acquired virtue. They also hold that attaining a higher end with more help is nobler than reaching a lower end alone.
claims: Beyond philosophy, a doctrine inspired by divine light is necessary because the end of human life is the immediate vision of God, to which philosophical knowledge is disproportionate.
Theology commands all other sciences and uses them in its service, since their ends are ordered to its end.
Philosophy and theology may treat the same beings, but under different formal rationes: creaturely reasons versus divinely inspired reasons.
Man's need for supernatural help reflects the superiority of his end, not a deficiency of his nature.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e885.summary: Article 2 asks whether there should be only one doctrine besides the physical disciplines. The objections argue for a plurality: the philosophical sciences are many, so divinely grounded sciences should be too. God and creature share no common genus. Moral and natural objects belong to different sciences. The sed contra arguments answer that whatever agrees in one ratio belongs to one science, and that divine science considers all things under the divine ratio, since all are from God and toward God. They add that Scripture mixes moral, theological, and cosmological matters within single books. In the response, Aquinas holds that the higher a cognition, the more unified and extensive it is, as God's intellect knows all things through one light. So sacred doctrine, grounded in divine inspiration, remains one while extending to diverse things in their specific character, which metaphysics cannot do through the merely common ratio of being. The replies add that the single divine light suffices for what the many philosophical sciences treat. They also hold that creator and creature are unified by an analogy in which the creature receives being and its ratio from the first being and imitates it, not by a common participated item prior to both. Finally, moral and natural objects fall under one science by the divine light, and theological virtue is in any case infused rather than produced by us.
claims: Sacred doctrine is one science, because its unity derives from the single divine light under which it considers all things.
The higher a cognition, the more unified it is and the more things it reaches; sacred doctrine thus exceeds metaphysics by knowing diverse things in their proper character.
Creator and creature are unified for a science not univocally but by an analogy of imitation, in which the creature receives being from the first being.
Virtue as treated by theology is infused by God, not produced by our agency.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e922.summary: Article 3 asks whether sacred doctrine is practical or speculative, and if speculative, whether it is science or wisdom. It is structured as three quaestiunculae, whose arguments are presented first and then answered in three corresponding responses. On the first question, Aquinas holds that sacred doctrine, perfecting both action and contemplation, is in a way both practical and speculative. It is principally speculative, however, since its ultimate end is contemplation of the first truth in patria, to which good works are a purification. On the second, it is a science. Its first principles are the articles of faith, self-evident to the believer through the infused light of faith, as natural principles are known through the agent intellect. It cannot prove these principles but can defend them, and it acquires a habit of the conclusions drawn from them, while faith itself functions as the unacquired habit of principles. Scripture's particular narratives serve as moral exemplars. On the third, it is most properly wisdom, and more divine than metaphysics, because it knows the highest causes through immediate divine inspiration and orders all other sciences. Against the objection from the uncertainty of faith, he holds that the believer's assent is firmer than assent to rational first principles. Faith's deficiency lies in the knower rather than in the certainty of its object, and reason led by faith grows toward understanding.
claims: Sacred doctrine is both practical and speculative, but principally speculative, because its ultimate end is contemplation of the first truth.

Sacred doctrine is a science whose first principles are the articles of faith, self-evident to believers by the light of faith; it defends rather than proves them and acquires a habit of their conclusions.
Sacred doctrine is most properly wisdom, more so than metaphysics, because it knows the highest causes through divine inspiration and orders all sciences.
The certainty of infused faith exceeds that of the first principles of reason; its deficiency is on the side of the knower.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e1098.summary: Article 4 asks what the subject of this science is, examining three candidate subjects, each paired with a counter-argument. These are God, who seems excluded by Boethius's principle that a simple form cannot be a subject; Hugh of St Victor's 'works of restoration', which seem excluded because theology also treats creation; and Lombard's 'things and signs', which seem excluded because other sciences treat them too. In the response, Aquinas distinguishes three conditions a subject must meet. It must contain all that the science treats, it must be what is principally known, and it must distinguish the science from others. He shows that earlier proposals, including the whole Christ and the credible, each satisfy only one of these conditions. As a subject satisfying all three, he proposes 'divine being knowable through inspiration'. Everything in theology is either God or what is from God and toward God as such, as medicine considers everything under its relation to health. Things are treated more principally the closer they come to the ratio of divinity. The replies then qualify each rival view. God is the subject as principally intended and as the ratio under which all is considered, and Boethius's principle concerns subjects of accidents, not subjects of predication. The works of restoration are the subject only insofar as everything is ordered to restoration, and things and signs only insofar as they are divine.
claims: A science's subject must contain all its contents, be principally known, and distinguish the science from others.
The subject of sacred doctrine is divine being knowable through inspiration: God, and all things insofar as they are from and toward God.
God can be the subject of a science as a subject of predication, even though a simple form cannot be a subject of accidents.
Rival proposals (works of restoration, things and signs, the whole Christ, the credible) capture only partial aspects of the subject.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e1140.summary: Article 5 asks whether the mode of proceeding of sacred doctrine is artful (artificialis). The objections argue that the noblest science should have the most artful mode, that a supremely unified science should have a single mode, that the truest science should not share poetry's metaphors, and that faith excludes argument (Ambrose). The sed contra arguments cite 1 Peter 3:15 and Titus 1:9, which require giving reasons and refuting opponents. In the response, Aquinas derives the multiple modes of sacred doctrine from the conditions of its matter. Revealed principles call for a revelatory mode on God's side and a prayerful one on the recipient's. Specifying faith through preaching confirmed by miracles calls for narrating signs. Principles exceeding reason in via call for a metaphorical or symbolic mode. The three ends to which the doctrine proceeds also have their modes: refuting error calls for argument; instructing morals calls for precept, threat, promise, and narrative example; contemplating truth in questions calls for argument again, as in the Fathers and in the Sentences. On this he grounds the fourfold sense of Scripture (historical, moral, allegorical, anagogical), adding that only the literal sense supports argument, since symbolic theology is not argumentative. The replies redefine 'artful' as 'fitted to the matter', so that this mode is supremely artful. They also reconcile unity of science with plurality of modes. Poetry and theology share the symbolic mode because neither is proportioned to reason, the one below it and the other above it. Finally, arguments cannot prove the articles but serve to defend the faith and to draw out truths from its principles.
claims: The mode of a science must follow the conditions of its matter; the many modes of sacred doctrine are thus fitting, and in that sense supremely artful.
Sacred doctrine's modes follow from the revealed and supra-rational character of its principles and from the ends it serves: refuting error, instructing morals, and contemplating truth.
The fourfold sense of Scripture corresponds to these ends, and only the literal sense supports argument.
Theology and poetry share the symbolic mode because neither matter is proportioned to reason, though for opposite reasons.
Argument cannot prove the articles of faith but is properly used to defend them and to infer truths from them.

ta-l1prolq1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium is Aquinas's commentary on Peter Lombard's prologue to the Sentences, together with the transition to the quaestio proper. Aquinas reads Lombard's prologue as a classical exordium that makes the reader benevolent, docile, and attentive. He analyzes Lombard's motives as a contest between moving causes, which express charity toward God and neighbor, and restraining causes; the contest is won by zeal for the house of God. He identifies the four causes of the work: its end (refuting error and manifesting truth), its efficient cause (God principally and Lombard instrumentally, as compiler of authorities), its matter (testimonies of truth), and its form (four books, and a method of examples and reasons). Throughout, he glosses Lombard's images and resolves brief dubia on presumption, adding to Scripture, knowing one has charity, and why truth is hated. He then sets out the five questions on sacred doctrine that follow: its necessity, its unity, its practical or speculative character, its subject, and its mode.
claims: Lombard's prologue is structured as an exordium rendering the reader benevolent, docile, and attentive.
Lombard compiled the Sentences out of charity toward God and neighbor, to refute error and manifest truth, with God as principal and himself as instrumental cause.
Exposition that unfolds what Scripture implicitly contains is laudable, not a forbidden addition.
Inquiry into sacred doctrine requires five questions: necessity, unity, practical or speculative character, subject, and mode.

ta-l1prolq1.summary: Aquinas's opening quaestio on sacred doctrine, prefaced by his commentary on Lombard's prologue, is a foundational account of the nature of theology. It answers the five questions announced in the Prooemium. Article 1 argues that a doctrine beyond philosophy is necessary, because the end of human life is the immediate vision of God, which creaturely knowledge cannot reach. A knowledge inspired by divine light is therefore needed in via, and it commands all other sciences and uses them as servants. Article 2 argues that this doctrine is one science, because the single divine light under which it considers all things lets it extend to diverse objects in their proper character, which metaphysics cannot do. Creator and creature fall under it through an analogy of imitation rather than univocity. Article 3 argues that it is principally speculative, being ordered to contemplation of the first truth. It is a genuine science whose first principles are the articles of faith, self-evident to the believer through the light of faith. And it is most properly wisdom, more divine than metaphysics, with a certainty that exceeds that of rational first principles. Article 4 identifies its subject as divine being knowable through inspiration: God, and all things insofar as they are from and toward God. Article 5 derives its many modes (revelatory, narrative, symbolic, argumentative, preceptive, and so on) and the fourfold sense of Scripture from the conditions of its matter and its ends, reserving argument to the literal sense. The whole presents theology as a unified, principally contemplative science that rests on revealed principles, is ordered to beatific vision, and subordinates the philosophical disciplines to itself.
claims: Sacred doctrine is necessary beyond philosophy because humanity's ultimate end, the immediate vision of God, exceeds what creaturely reasons can attain.
Sacred doctrine is one science, unified by the divine light under which it considers all things, and it commands and uses all other sciences.
Sacred doctrine is principally speculative, a true science grounded on the articles of faith as principles, and most properly wisdom.
Its subject is divine being knowable through inspiration: God and all things as related to God.
Its many modes and the fourfold sense of Scripture follow from the revealed, supra-rational character of its principles and from its ends, with argument proper to the literal sense.
